h1: Fibreglass and Double-Wall Oil Tanks for Newfoundland Homes
heroSub: About $650 more than steel buys a tank with a tag that can run decades instead of a dozen years. Free written estimates across St. John's and the Avalon, licensed and insured, and the same number answers 24/7 if your tag has already expired.
introHtml:
A fibreglass oil tank in Newfoundland is the closest thing to a buy-it-once purchase a homeowner can make for their heating system. Under the province's heating oil tank rules, a steel tank gets a tag good for 10 to 25 years depending on how it's built. A fibreglass or double-wall tank gets a service life set by the administrator instead, and that can run as long as 50 years. We've seen fibreglass tags stamped out to 2061.

Harbour Tank Co installs fibreglass and Roth double-wall tanks across St. John's and the Avalon, from Mount Pearl and Paradise out to Conception Bay South, Torbay and Bay Roberts. The upgrade runs about $650 more than a steel tank, roughly $3,850 installed against $3,200, and it buys two to three times the service life. Every job starts with a free written estimate, and we're licensed and insured. Call (709) 800-3117 or read on to see whether the upgrade makes sense for your house.

sections.heading: Why fibreglass and double-wall tanks get longer tags in Newfoundland
sections.html:
Newfoundland and Labrador's heating oil tank regulations set the clock on every tank in the province. Under section 15(1), a steel tank's life is fixed by how it's built and runs from 10 to 25 years. When that date passes, your oil supplier won't fill you, which is how a lot of St. John's families first hear about their tag in the middle of January.

Fibreglass and double-wall tanks are handled differently. Section 15(5) leaves their service life to the administrator, with a ceiling of 50 years. In practice that means the tag on a new fibreglass tank can be stamped decades out. We've seen fibreglass tags dated as far out as 2061.

That's the whole case for the upgrade in one line: instead of planning a replacement every 10 to 25 years, you likely install once and forget about it. If your current tag is close or already past, start with our expired tank emergency page and we'll sort the timing.

sections.heading: What the extra $650 buys you
sections.html:
The numbers are simple. A steel tank installed runs about $3,200. A fibreglass tank installed runs about $3,850. That's roughly $650 more up front for two to three times the service life.

Spread over the years the tank actually lasts, fibreglass comes out well ahead:

  • Steel at $3,200 over a 10 to 25 year tag works out to somewhere between $128 and $320 a year, and you'll buy another one when it expires.
  • Fibreglass at $3,850 over a tag that can run 50 years works out to as little as $77 a year, with no second install on the horizon.
  • The removal you skip. Every replacement means paying to pull and dispose of the old tank again. One long-life tank means one removal, not two or three.

Salt air pushes the math further in fibreglass's favour. An outdoor steel tank in Torbay, Pouch Cove or along the Conception Bay shore is fighting corrosion from day one, and coastal tanks often show rust at the seams and legs well before the tag date. Fibreglass doesn't rust, so the tank you buy is the tank you keep. Full pricing for every tank type is on our oil tank replacement cost page.

sections.heading: Indoor or outdoor: where your new tank should go
sections.html:
Where the tank sits changes which tank we recommend. Outdoors, fibreglass is the clear pick on the Avalon. It shrugs off salt air, freeze-thaw and the wet spring we get every year, and rust is one problem you can cross off the list.

Indoors, in a basement or utility room, the Roth double-containment tank is the one we fit. It's a seamless plastic inner tank sitting inside a galvanized steel outer shell that can hold the inner tank's full volume if it ever leaks. That double wall is why it qualifies for the same administrator-set life as fibreglass, and its upright shape fits most furnace rooms without crowding them.

A few things we check on the visit before we recommend a spot:

  • Distance from the fill pipe and vent to windows, doors and the property line.
  • Whether the existing pad or base is level and solid, or needs rebuilding.
  • Access for the delivery truck's hose, especially on the narrow older streets downtown.
  • Whether the fuel line to the furnace should be replaced along with the tank.

If you're not sure which way to go, that's what the free written estimate is for. We'll look at your setup in Mount Pearl, Paradise, Conception Bay South, Torbay, Portugal Cove-St. Philip's or Bay Roberts and put both options in writing.

sections.heading: 100-gallon fibreglass tanks for heat-pump homes
sections.html:
A lot of houses across St. John's and the Avalon have switched to a heat pump and kept the oil furnace as backup for the coldest stretches. If that's you, a full-size tank is more oil than you'll burn in a season, and more money than you need to spend. A 100-gallon tank installs for about $3,100 and gets the same long fibreglass tag.

The smaller tank still gives you a real safety net. When the heat pump loses ground in a February cold snap, the furnace has fuel and the supplier can top you up because your tag is valid. You also avoid the old problem of a big tank of stale oil sitting half-used for years.

Whichever size you choose, the job runs the same way. We remove the old tank, set the new one, connect and test the lines, and leave you with the paperwork your oil supplier needs on file. If you've already decided and just want it done, head to our oil tank replacement page or call (709) 800-3117.

faq.q: How long does a fibreglass oil tank last in Newfoundland?
faq.a: Under section 15(5) of the province's heating oil tank regulations, a fibreglass or double-wall tank gets a service life set by the administrator, capped at 50 years. Steel tanks are limited to 10 to 25 years under section 15(1). We've seen fibreglass tags stamped as far out as 2061, so a tank you install now can outlast the furnace it feeds.

faq.q: How much more does a fibreglass tank cost than steel?
faq.a: About $650. A steel tank runs roughly $3,200 installed and a fibreglass tank about $3,850, both in Canadian dollars. Because fibreglass carries two to three times the service life, it works out cheaper per year of heat. The full breakdown by tank type is on our oil tank replacement cost page.

faq.q: Should I choose fibreglass or a Roth double-wall tank?
faq.a: It mostly comes down to where the tank lives. Outdoors we recommend fibreglass because it doesn't rust in salt air. Indoors we fit Roth double-containment tanks, which hold the inner tank's full volume in the steel outer shell if it ever leaks. Both get the administrator-set service life of up to 50 years, so you're not giving up longevity either way.

faq.q: Will salt air wreck an outdoor oil tank on the Avalon?
faq.a: It's hard on steel. Outdoor steel tanks in coastal spots like Torbay, Portugal Cove-St. Philip's and around Conception Bay corrode faster than the same tank inland, and it's common to see rust on the legs and seams well before the 10 to 25 year tag date. Fibreglass doesn't corrode, so it keeps its full life outdoors. If your tank sits within sight of the water, fibreglass is the safer buy.

faq.q: I have a heat pump and only use oil as backup. What size tank do I need?
faq.a: Most heat-pump homes do fine with a 100-gallon tank, which installs for about $3,100. That's usually enough to carry the furnace through the cold snaps when the heat pump can't keep up, without paying for a full-size tank of oil that sits for years. It gets the same long tag as any other fibreglass tank. We'll confirm the size suits your furnace and your usage during the free written estimate.
